title: The Trickster Gets Tricked
overview: Jacob reaches his uncle Laban's home, falls in love with Rachel, and is tricked into first marrying her older sister Leah, who longs for his love as she bears him four sons.

parts.label: Arriving at the well (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Jacob reaches Harran, his mother's homeland far to the northeast, where wells were often capped with a heavy stone to protect scarce water. It seems the local custom was to wait until every flock had gathered so the well was opened only once, perhaps to guard the water supply.

parts.label: Jacob meets Rachel (vv. 9-14)
parts.note: Jacob rolls the heavy stone away alone, waters his cousin Rachel's flock, then kisses her in greeting and weeps aloud, though the text never says why. Laban welcomes him as his own flesh and blood, in a scene that echoes how Jacob's mother Rebekah was found at a well years before.

parts.label: Seven years for Rachel (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: With no money for a bride price, the payment a groom normally gave the bride's family, Jacob offers seven years of work instead. The Hebrew word for Leah's eyes is unclear, perhaps meaning soft or delicate, but the point is plain: Jacob loved Rachel.

parts.label: The bride switch (vv. 21-25)
parts.note: On the wedding night Laban sends in Leah, probably veiled and in the dark, and Jacob discovers it only in the morning. Many readers notice the irony: Jacob once tricked his blind father by posing as his older brother, and now an older sister is passed off as the younger.

parts.label: A second wedding (vv. 26-30)
parts.note: Laban excuses himself with a local custom that the older daughter marries first, then gives Rachel too after the week-long wedding celebration, in exchange for seven more years of work. Marrying two sisters was later forbidden in Israel's law, and the chapters that follow show the strain it created.

parts.label: Leah's four sons (vv. 31-35)
parts.note: "Not loved" (older translations say "hated") means loved less, and the text says the LORD saw this and gave Leah children while Rachel had none. Each name plays on her words, from "seen" and "heard" to "attached," until with Judah, whose line would later include King David, she simply says she will praise the LORD.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jacob being deceived should be read as God's deliberate discipline for his own earlier deceit, or simply as the story honestly showing deception breeding deception without spelling out a divine verdict.
think: Why do people so often hope that doing or achieving something will finally make someone love them, the way Leah hoped with each son?
